# Acids, Bases and Indicators

## Core ideas and reasoning

An acid supplies hydrogen ions in aqueous solution, while an alkali supplies hydroxide ions. A base neutralises an acid and may be insoluble; an alkali is a soluble base. Acids turn blue litmus red and alkalis turn red litmus blue. Indicators change colour over a range of pH, so select an indicator suited to the reaction. Universal indicator estimates pH but does not directly measure concentration. At about 25°C neutral water has pH 7, acids below 7 and alkaline solutions above 7. Acid strength describes the extent of ionisation, while concentration describes amount per volume. A dilute strong acid is therefore possible. Neutralisation removes hydrogen and hydroxide ions to form water. Acid-carbonate reactions also release carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky. Avoid confusing a colour change with the identity of a substance; use suitable confirmatory tests and controls. For titration distinguish an indicator endpoint from the exact chemical equivalence point.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Distinguish a base from an alkali.

A base neutralises acid; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water to produce hydroxide ions. Copper(II) oxide is a base but not an alkali.

### Example 2

Distinguish a strong acid from a concentrated acid.

Strong describes near-complete ionisation in water. Concentrated describes a large amount of acid per unit volume. Strength and concentration are different properties.

### Example 3

Give the ionic equation for neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong alkali.

H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). Spectator ions are omitted because they do not change in this reaction.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
